source_text: Ταῦτα δὴ πάντα δηλώσας ἡμῖν ὁ Παῦλος, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὰ μὲν παρόντα πρόσκαιρα, τὰ δὲ μέλλοντα αἰώνια καλέσας, τὸν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως κινεῖ λόγον, οὕτω λέγων· Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος ἡμῶν οἰκία τοῦ σκήνους καταλυθῇ, οἰκίαν ἐκ Θεοῦ ἔχομεν ἀχειροποίητον, αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. στʹ. Ὅρα πάλιν καὶ ἐνταῦθα πῶς ταῖς λέξεσιν κέχρηται κυρίως, δι' αὐτῶν τῶν ὀνομάτων τὴν δύναμιν ἐμφαίνων τῶν νοημάτων. Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς σκῆνος τὸ σῶμα ἐκάλεσεν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πρόσκαιρον τῆς παρούσης ζωῆς ἡμῖν ἐνδεικνύμενος, καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον μεταβολὴν δηλῶν, μονονουχὶ λέγων· Τί στενάζεις καὶ δακρύεις, ἀγαπητὲ, ὅτι τύπτῃ καὶ ἐλαύνῃ καὶ εἰς δεσμωτήριον ἐμπίπτεις; τί θρηνεῖς τὰς κατὰ μέρος ταύτας κακώσεις, ὀφείλων τὴν ὁλόκληρον δέξασθαι κατάλυσιν τοῦ σώματος· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐχ ἁπλῶς τοῦ σώματος, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐν τῷ σώματι φθορᾶς; Ἵνα γὰρ δείξῃ, ὅτι αἱ κατὰ μέρος αὗται κακώσεις οὐ μόνον ἡμᾶς λυπεῖν οὐκ ὀφείλουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐφραίνειν, δείκνυσιν ὅτι ἡ καθολικὴ καὶ τελευταία καθαίρεσις, εὐχῆς ἔργον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν, τὴν διὰ τοῦ θανάτου κατάλυσιν οὕτω λέγων. Καὶ πάλιν· Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ στενάζομεν τῷ σκήνει, τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθοῦντες. Οἰκίαν δὲ σκήνους ἤτοι τὸ σῶμα δι' ἀμφοτέρων καλεῖ τῶν ὀνομάτων· ἢ οἰκίαν σκήνους τὰς οἰκίας ἐν αἷς κατοικοῦμεν, τὰς πόλεις, τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ παρόντος βίου. Καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς εἶπεν, Οἶδα, ἀλλ', Οἴδαμεν, καὶ τὴν τῶν ἀκουόντων προσλαμβάνων γνώμην. Οὐ περὶ πραγμάτων ἀμφιβαλλομένων διαλέγομαι, φησὶν, οὐδὲ περὶ τῶν ἀγνοουμένων, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ ὧν ἤδη τὴν πίστιν ἐδέξασθε, εἰς τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου πιστεύσαντες ἀνάστασιν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ σκηνώματα καλοῦμεν τῶν ἀπελθόντων τὰ σώματα. Καὶ ὅρα πῶς καὶ τῇ λέξει κυρίως κέχρηται. Οὐκ εἶπεν, Ἀνῃρέθη καὶ ἠφανίσθη, ἀλλὰ, Κατελύθη, δεικνὺς ὅτι καταλύεται, ἵνα φαιδρότερον, ἵνα λαμπρότερον ἀναστῇ. Εἶτα ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν πόνων καὶ τῶν ἐπάθλων ἐποιήσατο σύγκρισιν, ἀπὸ τῆς ποιότητος, ἀπὸ τοῦ χρόνου καὶ τῆς ποσότητος· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐνταῦθα ποιεῖ, τὸ μὲν πῖπτον σῶμα σκῆνος καλῶν, τὸ δὲ ἀνιστάμενον οἰκίαν· καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς, οἰκίαν, ἀλλ' αἰώνιον· καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς, αἰώνιον, ἀλλ' οὐράνιον, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ χρόνου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ τόπου δεικνὺς τὴν ὑπεροχήν. Αὕτη μὲν γὰρ ἐπίγειος, ἐκείνη δὲ οὐράνιος· αὕτη πρόσκαιρος, ἐκείνη αἰώνιος. Καὶ νῦν μὲν καὶ σώματος δεῖ καὶ οἰκημάτων ἡμῖν διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκός· τότε δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ σῶμα ἔσται καὶ οἴκημα, οὐ δεόμενον στέγης, οὐδὲ καλυμμάτων τινῶν, ἀντὶ πάντων ἀρκούσης αὐτῷ τῆς ἀφθαρσίας. Εἶτα δεικνὺς τὴν ὑπεροχὴν τῶν ἐναποκειμένων αὐτῷ ἀγαθῶν, φησί· Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ στενάζομεν τῷ σκήνει. Οὐκ εἶπε, Στενάζω, ἀλλὰ κοινὴν ποιεῖται τὴν γνώμην. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ, φησὶ, στενάζομεν, βουλόμενος αὐτοὺς εἰς τὴν οἰκείαν ἑλκύσαι φιλοσοφίαν, καὶ τῆς αὑτοῦ κρίσεως ποιῆσαι κοινωνούς. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ στενάζομεν, τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν τὸ ἐξ οὐρανῶν ἐπενδύσασθαι ἐπιποθοῦντες. Οὐκ εἶπεν ἁπλῶς, Ἐνδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' Ἐπενδύσασθαι· καὶ ἐπάγει· Εἴ γε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι, οὐ γυμνοὶ εὑρεθησόμεθα.
thought_title: The earthly tent and the heavenly dwelling
orientation: Paul has just called present things temporary and future things eternal, and now Chrysostom expounds his words about the body as a tent that is dissolved and replaced by a dwelling from God.
pass_a_gloss: Having made all these things clear to us, Paul, and having for this reason called the present things temporary and the future things eternal, sets in motion the discourse about the resurrection, speaking thus: For we know that if our earthly dwelling of the tent is dissolved, we have a dwelling from God not made by hands, eternal in the heavens. 6. See again here too how he has used the words precisely, showing through the very names the force of the thoughts. For he did not simply call the body a tent, but showing us the temporary character of the present life, and making clear the change for the better, all but saying: Why do you groan and weep, beloved, because you are beaten and driven and fall into prison? Why do you lament these partial afflictions, when you ought to receive the complete dissolution of the body; or rather not simply of the body, but of the corruption in the body? For in order to show that these partial afflictions not only ought not to grieve us, but even to gladden us, he shows that the universal and final demolition is for us a matter of prayer, speaking thus of the dissolution through death. And again: For indeed in this tent we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven. And he calls it dwelling of a tent, either calling the body by both names; or dwelling of a tent meaning the dwellings in which we live, the cities, the form of the present life. And he did not simply say, I know, but, We know, taking along also the judgment of the hearers. I am not discoursing about matters disputed, he says, nor about things unknown, but about things for which you have already received the faith, having believed in the resurrection of the Lord. For this reason we also call the bodies of the departed tabernacles. And see how he has used the word precisely. He did not say, It was destroyed and made to disappear, but, It is dissolved, showing that it is dissolved in order that it may rise again more radiant, in order that it may rise again more splendid. Then just as in the case of the labors and the prizes he made a comparison, from quality, from time and from quantity; so indeed here too he does, calling the falling body a tent, and the rising body a dwelling; and not simply a dwelling, but eternal; and not simply eternal, but heavenly, showing the superiority both from time and from place. For this one is earthly, but that one heavenly; this one temporary, that one eternal. And now indeed we need both a body and dwellings because of the weakness of the flesh; but then the same thing will be both body and dwelling, needing no roof, nor any coverings, since incorruption suffices for it in place of all things. Then showing the superiority of the goods stored up in it, he says: For indeed in this tent we groan. He did not say, I groan, but he makes the judgment common. For indeed in this tent, he says, we groan, wishing to draw them to his own philosophy, and to make them sharers of his own judgment. For indeed in this tent we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from the heavens. He did not say simply, To put on, but, To put on over; and he adds: If indeed, having put it on, we will not be found naked.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'tent' for the body as a temporary dwelling, and Chrysostom is explicitly expounding Paul's choice of this word.
The glossary requires 'dwelling' for the permanent heavenly habitation, and Chrysostom contrasts it with the temporary tent.
Chrysostom stresses that Paul chose this verb rather than 'destroyed' or 'made to disappear' to show the body is taken down in order to rise again more splendidly.
Chrysostom explicitly notes Paul did not say simply 'to put on' but 'to put on over', and the distinction matters for the argument that follows.
The glossary requires 'corruption' for the decay in the body that is dissolved, as distinct from the body itself.
The glossary requires 'incorruption' for the state that suffices for the risen body in place of roof and coverings.

pass_b_english: After making all these things clear to us, Paul calls the present things temporary and the future things eternal, and then he sets in motion his argument about the resurrection. He says: “For we know that if our earthly dwelling of the tent is dissolved, we have a dwelling from God, not made by hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

Notice again here how precisely he uses his words, showing the force of his thoughts through the very names he chooses. He did not simply call the body a tent. He did so to point out to us the temporary character of our present life and to make clear the change for the better. He is all but saying: Why do you groan and weep, beloved, because you are beaten and driven out and thrown into prison? Why do you lament these partial hardships, when you ought to welcome the complete dissolution of the body—or rather, not simply of the body, but of the corruption in the body?

To show that these partial hardships not only should not grieve us but should actually make us rejoice, he shows that the complete and final taking down is something we pray for. That is why he speaks of the dissolution that comes through death. And again: “For in this tent we groan, longing to put on over it our dwelling place from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2).

He calls it “the dwelling of the tent,” meaning either the body by both names together, or “the dwelling of the tent” meaning the houses in which we live, the cities, the whole shape of this present life. And he did not simply say “I know,” but “we know,” drawing his hearers into his own conviction. “I am not discussing matters that are in doubt,” he says, “nor things that are unknown, but things for which you have already received the faith, since you have believed in the resurrection of the Lord.” That is why we also call the bodies of those who have departed “tents.”

Notice how precisely he uses the word. He did not say, “It is destroyed and made to disappear,” but “It is dissolved,” showing that it is dissolved so that it may rise again more radiant and more splendid. Then, just as he made a comparison in the case of labors and prizes—from quality, from time, and from quantity—so he does here as well. He calls the body that falls a tent, but the body that rises a dwelling. And not simply a dwelling, but an eternal one. And not simply eternal, but heavenly, showing its superiority both from time and from place. For this one is earthly, but that one is heavenly. This one is temporary, but that one is eternal.

Now we need both a body and houses because of the weakness of the flesh. But then the same thing will be both body and dwelling, needing no roof and no coverings of any kind, since incorruption will be enough for it in place of everything.

Then, showing the superiority of the good things stored up in it, he says: “For in this tent we groan.” He did not say, “I groan,” but he makes the conviction a shared one. “For in this tent,” he says, “we groan,” wanting to draw them into his own way of thinking and make them partners in his judgment. “For in this tent we groan, longing to put on over it our dwelling place from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2). He did not say simply “to put on,” but “to put on over.” And he adds: “If indeed, having put it on, we will not be found naked” (2 Corinthians 5:3).

problems.why: εὐχῆς ἔργον = 'object of prayer/wish,' not 'long for'
problems.fix: something we pray for, the object of our wish

fixed: Changed 'something we should long for' to 'something we pray for' because εὐχῆς ἔργον means 'a matter of prayer' or 'object of prayer,' not 'longing.'

last_rejected.why: Source marks verse 6 (στʹ = 6), not verse 1; citation should be 2 Cor 5:6 or section marker, not 5:1.
last_rejected.ruling: στʹ is a section/stichos marker, not a verse number; 2 Cor 5:1 is the correct scripture reference for the quoted text.

last_rejected.fix: owing to the complete dissolution of the body—or rather, not simply of the body, but of the corruption in the body
last_rejected.ruling: ὀφείλων with accusative + infinitive means 'ought to'; 'you ought to welcome' is correct and standard.

last_rejected.fix: an object of prayer for us
last_rejected.ruling: εὐχῆς ἔργον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν naturally means 'is for us a work of prayer' = 'something we pray for'; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: the complete and final taking down
last_rejected.why: καθαίρεσις here means 'dissolution/demolition,' not 'taking down' as if removing a tent; this obscures the death-resurrection parallel.
last_rejected.ruling: καθαίρεσις can mean 'taking down/demolition'; 'taking down' fits the tent metaphor and does not obscure the parallel.
